The Minister refers to his colleague, the Minister of Finance. 1 doubt whether people in his constituency or other farmers in western Canada would be in the same congratulatory mood.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON FARM FORECLOSURES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON FARM FORECLOSURES
speechtext: Under the circumstances I will direct my third question to the Minister of State for Finance. She knows that farmers are now paying about $1.1 billion annually in interest rates. Since she has been so generous to the depositors in the western banks, to the tune of $1 billion, would she convene her friends in the banking industry and arrange a moratorium on foreclosures in western Canada until this crisis is over?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON FARM FORECLOSURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me just point out two rather important pieces of information to the Right Hon. Member since he seems to have missed them. First, we had another decline in interest rates today which is of great benefit to farmers.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON FARM FORECLOSURES
speechtext: He just said that.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON FARM FORECLOSURES
speechtext: Second, many of the depositors in those banks were farmers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. As he may well know, if a farmer in southern Manitoba were to find some way of moving his land across the border to North Dakota he would not only receive double the value for his wheat, he would get cheaper machinery, fuel, and chemicals. This crisis calls for a totally co-ordinated approach covering all aspects of the farm cost price squeeze. Would the Prime Minister undertake to put that co-operative plan into place to look at things like reducing the fuel tax for farmers and providing a deficiency payment so that they can at least have a chance to compete in top world markets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member talked about a coordinated approach. He should know that the U.S. Farm Bill was put in place not solely by the administration but by the Congress as well. We have gone across the line to speak to farm groups and we have encouraged farm groups in Canada to do the same.
As I understand it, the Hon. Member had a chance to participate in the Canada-U.S. Parliamentary Association meeting which occurred at the end of February and the beginning of March. I would like to know if he took the concerns he is raising now on behalf of farmers to the U.S. Congressmen to see what kind of response he would get. If we are going to have a co-ordinated approach, 1 would like to know if he has been participating in seeing that that coordinated approach comes about.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MEETING OF GRAIN EXPORTING COUNTRIES
INTERNATIONAL MEETING OF GRAIN EXPORTING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again those people are abdicating their responsibilities and asking us to form the Government. We would be quite happy to take on that responsibility.
My supplementary question is again directed to the Prime Minister. The Minister of State for the Wheat Board has said that he expects there to be an international meeting this summer of all the export grain producing nations. In his discussions with President Reagan did the Prime Minister gain the agreement of the President for American participation in that conference, and did he also get the President's agreement that the Americans will co-operate in trying to find an international solution to this very deep and devastating problem affecting our farmers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MEETING OF GRAIN EXPORTING COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member talked about abdicating responsibilities. He should know that, as a result of a Government of which he was a part, which totally abdicated fiscal responsibility, we saw interest rates go as high as 20 per cent and that put a lot of farmers on their backs. We have a Minister of Finance who today is able to see the bank rate go under 9 per cent. That tells me that there is some responsibility on behalf not only of farmers but of everyone else in the country.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a question for the Minister. He said earlier that the Government would soon have something to say about stabilization payments. The Minister knows that there is a major distinction between that and deficiency payments. Since the Governments of the United States and European countries are doing a lot for their farmers to enable them to keep their farms and to keep producing, much more than our Government is in the present
April 10, 1986

crisis, will our Government announce a deficiency payment soon in order to put our farmers into a competitive position?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the beginning of the growing season and it is a long way away from being completed. Admittedly it is bad news at the beginning because of world grain prices over which Canada has very little control.
The President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the largest grain handling company in the country, said that "only crop insurance, grain stabilization and other agricultural programs kept the provincial farm economy from plunging into the red in 1985," and that in 1985 farm income showed "a net loss of $405 million when payments from these Government-supported programs aren't considered". We have been aware of the serious situation in agriculture and, as Mr. Turner said, without the help we gave in 1985, prairie farmers would have been in the red. That is the kind of record we have had in the past and we want to see what we can do to see that that record survives into the next year.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister referred to what Mr. Turner said last year. I will refer to what he said the day before yesterday. The day before yesterday he said that prairie farmers needed $1 billion from the Government. The Government did it for the banks. It should do it for the farmers now.
Hear, hear!

Would the Minister deal with that substantive question? Considering that the Europeans and Americans are helping their farmers, and considering that the Government bailed out the banks when they were in need, will he bring in a deficiency payment to help out our farmers who are now in need?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not accept the premise of the Hon. Member's question. By listening to him, one would think that the federal Government has done nothing for farmers. In fact there have been over 100 initiatives for farmers involving several billions of dollars.
As 1 said yesterday and on previous occasions-and if the Hon. Member wants to do the arithmetic, I will give him the figures after Question Period-the amount of money the federal Government put directly into the prairie grain economy in 1985 amounted to something like $1.5 billion. We have seen the problem, and we have acted by transferring literally billions of dollars to the western economy.

Mr. Speaker, the crisis that is being faced now is in 1986. The Minister was talking about 1985.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister. On the eve of the last general election, in Prince Albert, appropriately enough, he made a number of promises on behalf of his Party to the agricultural sector. Among them was the promise to remove all federal taxes from farm fuels. Since at least four cents per litre has not been rebated to farmers, will the Prime Minister at least live up to his promise which he made in the Prairies to farmers, and remove all federal taxes from farm fuels?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member was reading the wrong document. The document to which he should more accurately refer suggested that we would remove the sales tax from farm fuels. If he checked the record, he would see that we did that. In fact we did it about three days after this House convened after the election.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board. In the last general election the Prime Minister made a campaign commitment that he would make Canada into a superpower in terms of agricultural exporting nations. How can the western farmer even survive with the initial price announced this week, it being the lowest since 1930 in terms of purchasing power back in the days of R. B. Bennett and Bennett buggies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in terms of Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier of high quality food products around the world, Canada has an extremely good reputation. The Canadian Wheat Board has a very good reputation of being able to sell and maintain our markets. The Canadian Grain Commission has a reputation second to none. It is one of the oldest and most respected agencies in terms of grading and quality of grain in the world. We have maintained that reputation. The problem we face is not unique to Canada and Canadian farmers. The problem we face is a larger problem, that is, very depressed world grain prices.

Mr. Speaker, why is the Government not prepared to provide 1985 initial prices which would provide about $1 billion worth of support to western farmers who are in serious financial difficulty? The Minister knows that during the last several weeks, or a month or so, we have advanced several billions of dollars to support banks in trouble. Why can we not give the same kind of support and assistance to farmers who are in deep trouble?

April 10, 1986
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to say again and again that we have been spending many, many millions, in fact billions of dollars, in terms of the federal Government's support to Canadian agriculture. Let me also tell the Hon. Member what some people in the grain business are saying. He talked about raising prices to the 1985 level, which everyone would like to see return. Here is what some people are saying: "Please tell the farmer the truth and don't use initial prices to mislead him". That is what we tried to do. We have tried to be as honest and as straightforward as possible in the very serious situation which we face in world grain prices.
As I pointed out, the Government has a good record in terms of seeing the problem, being able to address it, and of the amount of money which has been transferred from the federal Government to the grain economy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. The Prince Albert Declaration indicated that they would remove the 9 per cent sales tax and all the excise tax. Will the Minister now tell us that they will do exactly that?
Mr. Speaker, that action was taken so long ago that I would have to check the record, but my memory would lead me to believe that indeed that has been done.
Ask the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, along the same lines of agricultural finance, would the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board at least consider the payment of a deficiency payment?
I think the Hon. Member knows that that is not a supplementary question. The Hon. Member for Papineau.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. What guarantees can he give this House that today, as he promises to tighten security in our airports, his credibility is any better than it was on June 25, 1985, after the Air India tragedy, when he announced that exceptional air safety measures would be taken?

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the Hon. Member yesterday, a number of steps have been implemented and a number of steps
are under review. Airports across the country are undergoing audits. I also indicated yesterday the additional steps we would be taking in view of the very serious issue which occurred last week. I take this matter as a very serious one. I indicated that 1 would be calling in the executives of the airlines and the Burns security people. As well, I will be inviting representatives of the unions to sit down to see what further steps can be taken to ensure the highest level of safety at all airports throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Minister jumping on his feet to try to save the credibility of the Prime Minister.
Oh, oh!

Could the Minister of Transport tell us whether it is true that 100 recommendations were made a long time ago that are now before Cabinet and before the Government for study, and that the Government has not yet taken any action because of costs? The Government is now nickel-and-diming with the lives and the security of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, first, 1 will put the credibility of this Prime Minister against any past or future Prime Minister.
Hear, hear!
We will take a bet.
Tell John Fraser that.
Order, please.

To respond to the serious part of the Member's question, as I said yesterday, the Solicitor General and myself are in the process of preparing a joint memorandum to Cabinet which will provide for a comprehensive security enhancement program at all our airports. I am sure the Hon. Member will be very interested in that.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN AND UNITED STATES GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. He knows that the United States floor price for grain is $145 a tonne Canadian, and that the announcement the Wheat Board made in this country for initial prices works out to $130 Canadian.
Why is the initial price for Canadian grain $15 or $10 lower in Canada than in the United States when the U.S. floor price
April 10, 1986

in reality becomes the world floor price? Why is there a $15 shortfall for Canadian farmers? It is not necessary, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
subsubtopic: CANADIAN AND UNITED STATES GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not so sure the Hon. Member does his arithmetic correctly. There is more to setting prices than simply looking at the U.S. rate. Also, if the Member wants to get into the U.S. Farm Bill, he will know that it is a very complex piece of legislation. I have said previously, and I will say again, that we do not want to be totally spooked by the U.S. Farm Bill. We want to look at the bigger problem and look at it in context with what the Europeans are doing.
We have set, to say it again, the initial prices this year at probably a higher percentage of the anticipated realized final price than has been the case in the past.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board knows that this morning we had a striking committee on a special study of parity pricing and a higher domestic wheat price.
Can the Minister say whether or not he is now prepared to make a recommendation that we have a parity price for Canadian grain sold to Canadians for domestic purposes and that we adjust it annually according to the increase in the cost of production?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is appropriate for anybody to prejudge what the committee will find. What I said on Tuesday, and say again, is that we want to look very seriously at raising prices for domestic consumption.
What the hell is your policy?

We give credit to the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville and also to the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, for this is something we want to look at very seriously.
I quoted before the President of the Consumers Association of Canada, Mrs. Sally Hall from Edmonton. Anytime we have gone to consumers with our case and consumers understand where the money is going, we have been treated very fairly by them. That, however, is up to the committee. Whatever the committee recommends, as far as the Government is concerned, we will be prepared to take a very serious look at it.

subsubtopic: EXPENDITURES ON JOB TRAINING IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:

Why, in the last fiscal year when $55 million was approved for job creation and job training in British Columbia, was only $40 million spent? Why, Mr. Speaker?

April 10, 1986
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: EXPENDITURES ON JOB TRAINING IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will know that, indeed, the situation in British Columbia is serious with regard to unemployment, but he will also recognize that since this Government came to office 60,000 new jobs have been created in the Province of British Columbia.
In the past year some $260 million alone has been spent by the Department of Employment on programs to assist individuals and organizations in the Province of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, there are 50,000 fewer people employed in British Columbia today than there were in 1981. There are 5,000 fewer people employed on Vancouver Island than when this Government came into office.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT SIMPLIFIED TAX RETURN FORM BE DEVISED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question today is for the Minister of National Revenue. One way American citizens cope with the complicated personal income tax system is with a special one-page tax return for filers with few deductions, called 1040EZ. Can the Minister tell the House whether it would be possible to provide over 10 million eligible Canadian taxpayers with similar and much needed tax simplification?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT SIMPLIFIED TAX RETURN FORM BE DEVISED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague knows that for many many millions of Canadians who are claiming tax credits, such as refundable sales tax or child tax credits, the T-l Special affords them an opportunity to simplify greatly their income tax filing. On the

Member for Mississauga South made reference to the contribution that the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs hopes to make in this regard, and I can assure him that our officials are also working very hard in conjunction with the Minister of Finance's officials in proceeding with this important task.

subsubtopic: REPORTED INVESTIGATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Prime Minister a question about the matter raised by my colleague and not answered by the Solicitor General. The Solicitor General has been silent about the matter but his officials have not. Officials of the RCMP have made official statements about the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: REPORTED INVESTIGATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I refer the hon. gentleman to the comments of his Leader made on November 30, 1984, reported on page 770 of Hansard. He said the following:
Would he-
-meaning my predecessor as Solicitor General-
-review the practice of his Department, and perhaps his own approach to investigations, by reinstating the practice that used to apply in this House, and I believe still should, reflecting the principle of presumption of innocence until proven guilty?

subsubtopic: REPORTED INVESTIGATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext: That has nothing to do with the question.

subsubtopic: REPORTED INVESTIGATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext: 1 expect that the Hon. Member would respect the wishes of his Leader, which were not to do that.

subsubtopic: REPORTED INVESTIGATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext: The issue has been raised by your own officers, Perrin, and that's quite different.

subsubtopic: REPORTED INVESTIGATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
That's right, get your facts straight.

I can only say that in interpreting this new guideline in the rule I hope you would give it broad interpretation and err on the side of permitting the motion that was defeated in the committee rather than keeping it out. If you do not do that, I suggest Hon. Members will begin to keep most of our key amendments for the report stage and not take a chance. I suggest this will simply clog the House with far more motions than you would otherwise get.
It has been my experience so far with the new legislative committees that little attention is paid to them. It is very difficult to reach the public in those committees because they are not covered by the press or television. In other words, one cannot have the impact on public opinion; whereas we can have impact to a certain extent in the House. If Members believe that every time they put a motion in the legislative committee and it is defeated it cannot be dealt with here, they will simply reserve and put them here. Therefore, I would argue for a broad interpretation of that rule.
You also stated in your ruling that it would be your intention to rule these motions out of order and you referred Hon. Members to Citation 773(10) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition. That citation reads as follows:
A substantive amendment may not be introduced by way of a modification to the interpretation clause of a bill.
I would argue that two of the motions to amend which you say you intend to rule out of order are not substantive amendments to the interpretation clause because the interpretation clause of the Bill simply says:
"employer" means any person who employs one hundred or more employees-
We simply changed the number from 100 to 25. So we are not really changing the substance of the interpretation section but suggesting simply that the level be changed. I would ask you to reconsider that submission.
Finally, in point 13 of your ruling you say:
Motion numbered 33A would have the effect of enlarging the duties of the Human Rights Commission by making it a partner with the Minister in the preparation of reports under the provisions of the Bill.
In committee the Government agreed to an amendment which brought in the operation of the Human Rights Commission. All we are doing simply is refining that new provision which the Government itself provided. I would respectfully ask that the Chair give some consideration to the points 1 have made.

Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-62, be amended in Clause 2 by striking out line 6 at page 1 and
substituting the following therefor:
"2. The purpose of this Act is to promote and encourage".
He said: Mr. Speaker, we now begin the next stage of Bill C-62. This debate has been going on for over a year since we first received the report of Judge Rosalie Abella. Judge Abella was appointed by the former Government when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) was the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Judge Abella brought down with a very superb report. She stated that this country needed what she called "employment equity" for the majority of women as well as for the three minority groups, the disabled, natives and visible minorities.
We have gone through the preliminary stages. A Bill was introduced for first reading by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). We then had a second reading debate. We have gone through very extensive hearings in the parliamentary legislative committee. It has been an interesting and fascinating process.
I have proposed Motion No. 1 which deals with the purpose of the Bill. The purpose section of Bill C-62 states:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the work place so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfilment of that goal, to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada-
The key words in the purpose section are: "The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the work place".
I moved this amendment because I do not think this Bill will achieve equality in the workplace. I call as my witness to this fact the four target groups for which this Bill was planned. Several women came before the committee and all said to us that the Bill was not strong enough, what we needed were targets. The Bill does not have targets. They said we needed goals and timetables, but this Bill does not have these either. In addition to women, disabled Canadians came to committee and told us the Bill is not strong enough, that it does not have timetables, goals or objectives. In effect, this is not a Bill to achieve employment equity. It is a Bill to report on employment equity. There is a big difference.
I was proud of several disabled Canadians who came to this Parliament about a week and a half ago and waited outside the Conservative Caucus Committee room. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) came to the caucus they confronted him. They pleaded with him to strengthen Bill C-62. 1 remembered a blind Canadian, a deaf Canadian, and a very articulate woman from Toronto who was in a wheelchair. They spoke to the Prime Minister as part of a coalition against Bill C-62 as drafted. They pleaded with the Prime Minister to strengthen it. To his credit, the Prime Minister sent them up to
Employment Equity Act
see his policy adviser in the Prime Minister's Office. They spent about a half hour with him and were promised that a report will come back to them.
But I make an appeal now on behalf of disabled Canadians, one of the four target groups, that we strengthen Bill C-62. If we do not, we might just as well accept Motion No. 1, because my motion brings Bill C-62 in line with what it is really all about. My motion would change the words "to achieve employment equity" to the words "to promote and encourage employment equity", because all we see in the Bill is the reporting of employment equity, we do not see the achievement of employment equity. So on behalf of disabled Canadians I call upon the Goverment majority to persuade the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Prime Minister to bring us some targets, an enforcement agency and some goals and objectives so that employers will be made to achieve employment equity on behalf of women and disabled persons; that is what they asked for in committee.
I also call as witnesses the visible minorities. They came to our committee and contacted us in person by telephone and by letter. They also said the Bill was not strong enough. They want an enforcement agency, targets, goals and objectives. If these things are not written into law, because of the human psyche of the majority in our country and everywhere else in the world, these minorities will still be discriminated against.
My last witnesses are the original Canadians, the Indians, Metis and Inuit people of Canada or, as the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) used to call them in our constitutional committee a few years ago, the "prefounding Canadians". They are not the founding races such as the French and the English, but they are the ones who were here first of all. Those people spoke to us as a predominantly white, male-dominated Parliament, and said that this Bill is not strong enough and would only encourage and promote employment equity in reports on employment equity rather than achieve employment equity.

Believe it or not, Mr. Speaker, when the Conservative Party was elected to government, I was greatly optimistic that there would be a new era in Canadian politics.
Shame on you.
I am being shamed by my colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway, and she is right.
Vancouver East, but he's ashamed too.

When the Conservative Party was elected to govern, I thought that there would be more openness. I thought that Conservative Members would listen to various groups and draft legislation that ordinary Canadians wanted. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a solemn promise that he would do so. In fact, he made over 300 electoral promises on which Canadians elected him. Even new Members

The Bill before us has been drafted for the benefit of women, natives, disabled Canadians and visible minorities but all four groups say that it is not good enough. All four groups have rejected the Bill. Is that participatory democracy? A former Prime Minister used to talk a lot about participatory democracy. He lasted here for about 16 years before the people wisened up. Now members of the Conservative Party talk about the same thing without using those words. They said they would listen to the people and that there would be more openness in Government. They said that they would bring people into the centre of power and cut away the bureaucracy.
I know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is probably quite embarrassed by all this. Having been Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development at one time, he has a great feeling for native Canadians. I am sure that if he had drafted this Bill, it would be a stronger one. I know that he is a good progressive Tory and he would have drafted a stronger Bill.
There's no good Tory.
The Hon. Member seems to be very anti-Tory. She has said that there is no such thing as a good Tory.
There's a good suppository but not a good Tory.

Perhaps she is right, but I tend to be a bit more optimistic than that. I do think that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would have developed a more progressive Bill than did the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). Perhaps the Minister of National Health and Welfare could use his good offices and influences to try to persuade the Minister of Employment and Immigration to accept some amendments that would ensure that this Bill will listen to disabled Canadians and other targeted groups and include an enforcement agency and a maximum fine increased from $50,000. After all, what is $50,000 for the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Bank of Montreal or General Motors? It is peanuts.
We are going to have to get a lot tougher. We are going to have to have targets. As well, Government Departments will have to be brought into line with Bill C-62. I know that there are Treasury Board guidelines, but those guidelines are ignored. In fact, we heard in committee that over 75 per cent of disabled Canadians who work for the federal Government work on contract and are not full-time employees. When there are budget cut-backs, the contract employees are often the first to be let go. That is why disabled Canadians want a stronger Bill.
I know that many Conservative Members are afraid to take a stand against the big banks and large companies but I appeal to them to listen to the target groups for which we are trying to
draft legislation and to put into law the things that the groups are requesting. These groups are saying that they want collective bargaining to be implemented in this Bill so that workers in the different industries will have a guaranteed role to play in the implementation of employment equity. Women are telling us that they need equal pay for work of equal value. Like the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), 1 was not optimistic that the Conservative Government would listen to us about that, but perhaps we can make a few more appeals.
I see you are getting a little restless, Mr. Speaker. Last, on behalf of those four target groups, we want to have a tough provision in this Bill on contract compliance so that companies that sell goods or services to the Government of Canada will have to achieve employment equity or be cut off like you are trying to cut me off, Mr. Speaker. Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with a great deal of pride and humility in responding to the comments of my two hon. colleagues. I have lived my entire life in the milieu, although I am not a member of a visible minority, of a minority community. Through my lifetime I have been exposed to quotas. I can say honestly that I feel I am a worthy representative of all target groups which have been mentioned. Sixty per cent of all Canadians fall within that range. I represent a riding which is very heavily ethnic in its nature. My consultations with my supporters and the people who live in the riding of Dollard indicate to me how pleased they are with the Government, the first Government anywhere, having the guts to bring in legislation which will actually put into effect an employment equity program.
We want jobs. We know that when goals and timetables are put into effect, we will get those jobs because we are qualified. We do not want quotas. We do not want to focus upon process. We want results. We want initiative. We want a commitment to change. We want measureable goals. We get all this with employment equity.
Today I heard the request for a new enforcement agency. We are already involved in enough bureaucratic red tape. We are in the process of examining ways of dismantling some agencies. We know the high costs of governing. We already have in place the Canadian Human Rights Commission which
Employment Equity Act
is very well prepared to handle all cases of systemic discrimination resulting from employers not following the program we have put into effect.
My friend in the New Democratic Party wants us to put water in our wine before we ever begin. We are introducing today a mandatory program for the first time. The wording "to achieve equality" more correctly reflects the purpose of the Bill. What we are doing is achieving it. Promoting and encouraging are voluntary terms, and that is not what we see in the Bill. We want to see all groups move forward, not strictly by legislation because that is simply a process. We want to send out a signal of how productive society will become when we use the full constituent part of our community.
I am certainly completely against this motion. In terms of what might be the position of the two opposition Members, it has been a pot-pourri. In terms of all other motions, 1 know I will have an opportunity to speak on each one of them. April 10, 1986 is a proud day for us because we are sending out a signal to Canadians in all walks of life that from now on one's colour, sex, nationality or racial origin does not matter; if one is qualified, the job will be his or hers. We are doing it with an affirmative action program.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Motion No. 1 in amendment to Bill C-62. I am concerned with the remarks which the Parliamentary Secretary has just made.
1 am somewhat amazed that he should rise and say that he represents a minority which has suffered from the imposition of quotas and then imply that we do not need positive mechanisms to deal with the problem. He is making quotas, an example of enforcement machinery, a dirty word. He is using the same language for positive measures to promote real employment equity. He is trying, by guilt by association, to suggest that it is somehow discriminatory. He says that they want results, but we have Bill C-62 which will not bring results. He says that we have mandatory employment equity. It is not mandatory if there are no employment equity enforcement mechanisms. That has been made very clear. Judge Abella said that voluntary enforcement simply would not be adequate. It does not matter how much it is called mandatory. If there is no enforcement mechanism to make it work, it will not be truly mandatory.
I support the motion before us which calls the Bill really what it is. Turning to Clause 2 of Bill C-62, it reads;
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the workplace so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfilment of that goal, to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada-
That is certainly the objective. That would be fine, but since we do not have teeth or enforcement mechanisms in Bill C-62, the clause dealing with the purpose of the Act is misleading. It tells the public that employment equity will be achieved, but it
Employment Equity Act
will not be achieved until there are real tough mandatory provisions. The proposal of the NDP is simply to be honest about the Bill. It has good intentions, and that is all. Therefore, in part our amendment reads:
The purpose of this Act is to promote and encourage.
Of course it will promote and encourage employment equity. It is looking in the right direction. It has the right goal at the end, but it is just that it is in no hurry to get there. If we are to have effective enforcement of employment equity, we would have serious penalties for violation. However, Hon. Members will recall that the only penalty contained in Bill C-62 is a $50,000 fine, and $50,000 is peanuts for a company which is making a fortune by exploiting people and paying them less than they ought to be paid. The only penalty is for failing to report. There is no fine for failing to make progress in achieving employment equity. If this Bill were really about the achievement of employment equity, the fine would be in the failure to move ahead, the failure to see that women, visible minorities, handicapped people and native people really made it into the labour force in sizeable numbers, the numbers they deserve, not just token members here and there.
By comparing successive reports, the Minister hopes that the evidence will be sufficient for the Canadian Human Rights Commission to correct systemic discrimination identified by the reports. However, the Minister intends to rely heavily upon public opinion to persuade firms to remove discriminatory barriers which face women, native people, visible minorities and disabled persons. This is precisely the approach which was rejected by Judge Abella in her study. It is precisely the point made by representatives of organizations representing women, native people, disabled persons and visible minorities. They have said that this is not enough. Indeed, some of them said very strongly that we ought to vote against the whole Bill unless the Government is prepared to bring in amendments or to accept our amendments to put real teeth into it.
Public opinion will not work because profits are involved. People make money by paying victims in the market-place less. That is what they will do. They are not moved to change their practices. They are not moved to make reasonable accommodation to incorporate disabled persons. They are not moved to change their recruitment practices to find people who have not heretofore been available for that kind of work. All of that requires a bit of effort and a bit of money. Who is going to put forward that effort and money to bring their employment practices up to fair standards when they can go ahead without any fear of penalties by maintaining the practices that they already have?
We recommend that this Bill should include all Government Departments under federal jurisdiction as well. As it is written now, it applies only to federal Crown corporations. It does not extend to Ministries. At the very least, as a matter of principle, the Government should expect itself as an employer to follow these quite low expectations, not high enough expectations, but
April 10, 1986
surely that at least should be a requirement for the Government to follow.
Treasury Board guidelines are in place for affirmative action in the federal Public Service, but these have been very weak. They have not been effective. We have seen very little movement as a result. The guidelines can be changed. They are not subject to a statute. They can be changed without the matter coming to Parliament at all, whereas if the requirement were right in the Bill, then that could not happen without a new Bill being brought back into Parliament.
The Bill as it currently stands does not allow for adequate participation by labour unions, which have shown a great deal of sensitivity and willingness to work to achieve employment equity. Many of the employers who fall under federal jurisdiction have largely unionized workforces. We have asked that wherever a union is present in the workplace, the employer must bargain the implementation of employment equity. The Bill does not require this. It simply requires the employer to consult with the bargaining agent, but not to sit down seriously and work out a plan that is fair, reasonable and will be effective.
Throughout debate in the House and before committee we emphasized the importance of enshrining the concept of equal pay for work of equal value in this Bill. We moved amendments to this effect, but our amendments were rejected. The Abella Report was very clear that equal pay for work of equal value should be part of all equity programs. It is not here in the Bill.
Finally, I would like to point to contract compliance. We fought to have this added to the Bill. The answer we got was: "Well, we are going to go ahead with it anyway so we do not need a statute on this". But the provisions which the Government is planning to go ahead with are not as vigorous as they could be. They are limited to firms doing $200,000 or more worth of business with the Government and where the firm has more than 100 employees. It is a start, but why should it be restricted to only those companies?
If we really want to encourage employment equity and equal pay for work of equal value, we would extend that principle and use the bargaining power of a contract with Government to make more companies be fair in their employment measures. They would have a positive incentive for coming up with employment equity measures instead of relying on the same goodwill which we know has not been effective. If that had been effective, we would not need this Bill. Employment equity would already have been achieved and it would have been achieved years ago. But it has not.
What we are calling for is real teeth. Unless and until we get real teeth we think at the very least the Government should have the decency not to mislead the Canadian public and to call the Bill precisely what it is, namely, an attempt at goodwill to promote and encourage employment equity, but it should certainly not claim that it is a Bill that will achieve employment equity.

April 10, 1986

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to motion No. 1 which has been proposed to amend the text on the purpose of Bill C-62 from saying it is a Bill to achieve equality in the workplace to stating instead that it is a Bill to promote and encourage such equality.
The explanation given by the mover of this motion is that regrettably the Bill does not achieve the goals that are needed and, therefore, the Member proposes that we call it what it is and say that it is simply something to promote equality in the workplace, a very desirable thing.
I have to say that I do not want to support this motion because I feel that that would be a way to give satisfaction to the Conservatives. They would then be able to say that they had achieved something by saying that they were promoting something. We know they are not going to achieve a thing through this Bill, other than to deceive the public into thinking that they have done something. This is the regrettable part of this Bill. It will betray by delaying those people who are still waiting for their rights, rights which were promised to them under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, at least guaranteed to them by law if they take their cases to court. The Government, instead of now applying the provisions of that Charter, for which we had to fight so hard in the last Government, is postponing its implementation by making people think that by a long, circuitous action they will some day arrive at the promised land.
Some people say they are eternal optimists. They have to wait an eternity. One of the Tory Members said that she was an eternal optimist. Those people who have to wait, the handicapped, the deaf, or the blind do not want to wait for an eternity. They want action now. They want the kind of action that has been called for by all who are experts and knowled-gable in this field as to what the purpose of a Bill that brings about equality means. They want action that will have teeth in it.
Judge Abella brought a report forward. We had the Obstacles Report before that. Various reports in other countries have been made. All reports call for legislation to make it clear that the victim does not first have to prove his right to justice. It is up to the Government, if it has courage, to provide to people the kind of guarantee that they will have their rights protected.
After fighting for the Charter of Rights and Freedoms against the Tories during the last administration when they rang the bells, attacked the Chair and yelled and stood up hour after hour on various questions of privilege and points of order to stall and deter the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Constitution from being brought to this country, that same Party, in this kind of hypocritical stance, now pretends it will stand up for those rights and enforce them. It is not standing up for rights. It is not enforcing them. It is making a mockery of them.
Employment Equity Act
I heard the Parliamentary Secretary for Employment and Immigration (Mr. Weiner) speak about how he represents minority groups in his riding. I hope he will continue to try to represent them. I am sure he is sincere in believing in his heart that he is effectuating something helpful to them, but I want to tell him that I have worked for most of my life in human rights causes and as head of a human rights organization. One of the reasons I came to Parliament was to try to see the Charter of Rights and Freedoms brought into effect. One of the reasons I am in Parliament is to try to bring about those things that I saw needed to be done as head of a human rights organization.
I saw the discrimination that took place, the delays, and I saw the poor people who do not have the money to bring their cases to court. As a Government, we should provide effective machinery for them to carry their cause so they do not have to go to court to plead it. That should be the next step. The question must be asked, is that what is happening?
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in the field of human rights you will find that all minority groups, all oppressed groups, say that if you want to know whether or not something is good, ask us because we are the ones who suffer. We have heard the people. We have asked them. They have come to the committees. They have practically unanimously said that this Bill is not enough, it does not protect us.
I suggest that we should leave the word "achieve" right where it is. It is not as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration said. If we put in those other words, it would not be watering the Bill down to say, "to encourage". What the Member of the New Democratic Party was trying to do was to mock the Bill. That is why he did what he did. The Bill deserves to be mocked. I will not, therefore, support the idea of changing this to "encourage", but would rather leave it as "achieve" so that the record of history will judge them on what they did to help the people of the country who are handicapped, the women, the native people, and the minority groups.
Are they really satisfied in their hearts that they have done enough? I think they will not say that they have achieved nothing else but to ensure that some reports are sent in. Is that what they are going to do? They are giving companies three years to make reports. If the reports are not made, they will be fined $50,000, but if they do make a report, it will be okay. That is the kind of enforcement this Bill gives us. They can dilly-dally in the courts indefinitely with regard to what that report said and did.
This a tragic travesty. I hope that when the Government comes to its senses it will either change this Bill or accept the condemnation of all of these groups: women, minorities of various racial backgrounds, visible minorities, native people, and the handicapped.

April 10, 1986
Employment Equity Act
