The House resumed consideration of Bill C-62, an Act respecting Employment Equity, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee, and Motion No. I (Mr. Nystrom) (p. 12098).

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me today to have the opportunity to comment on the employment equity Bill as it moves into report stage. I have been interested and involved in this Bill since its inception and through the committee stage. It is a very proud moment for me and my colleague, the parliamentary Secretary to the Minister, to be here today as the Bill goes through its final stage in the House and becomes reality.
The Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) referred to a Member who has been referred to as an optimist. 1 am that Member. Yes, 1 am an optimist, and I am proud of it. I am proud of this country and I am proud of Canadians. I believe that Canadians support the concept of employment equity, and it is Canadians who will make it work rather than government. Social change does not come about merely because government decrees it. This kind of social change comes out of the consciousness of Canadians. We, as legislators, provide moral leadership, but Canadians themselves, who recognize inequity, are prepared to make the changes which will be so important.
If we are going to mock anything, I think we should mock the horrendous record of the opposition Party which was in power for almost 20 years and did not do anything to ameliorate the conditions of inequity in the workforce. It had lots of opportunity, but did nothing. In a mere 18 months the Progressive Conservative Government has put this proposal forward, has listened to the people of the country, and is achieving results.
Hear, hear!

The purpose of this Bill is to achieve equality, and 1 believe it will do that, for a number of reasons. Those of us who have been involved in the committee are aware of the process. Employers will be required to report on their progress in employment, training, and promotion of people from the target groups. Data will be available to which companies may compare their figures with the number of people available in the community with those qualifications. It will be quite an easy process and it will be on the public record.
There will be, first of all, the public assessment. I know that some of my colleagues in the Opposition pooh-pooh that and say it does not matter. I do not agree with them. Public assessment will operate in two ways. People who are concerned can respond with their dollars. They can withdraw from purchasing the goods or services of those companies which do not fully participate and achieve employment equity. There are other interesting things which I am sure my colleagues are aware of.
In my own hometown of Vancouver, the Vancouver City Savings Credit Union and a private sector group have already new investment funds in place which they will only invest in socially responsible companies. Part of the criteria will be that companies implement and achieve employment equity. That kind of recognition is taking place out in the market-place. That is not Government telling people to do it. Canadians are saying that they think it is right, and they will achieve it themselves.
This piece of legislation is perhaps a carrot on a stick. Being the optimist that I am, I really believe in the carrot. I certainly think this legislation provides that carrot. The companies will have to make their reports, and they will have to start to examine themselves. They will have to start to put in place proper human resource management policies in order to achieve equality. They will have to reach out into the community.
As I said in committee so often, if we spent less of our time arguing about the process and procedure, and more of our time getting representatives of the target groups together with the employers to talk about how we are going to do this, we would achieve more. I recommended this to representatives of the target groups and companies. They said that, since they were not quite sure of what they should be doing, they would like to talk to people in those groups. If we used that co-operative, consultative approach, I think we could achieve employment equity even without the stick which we have in this piece of legislation.
There is no stick.

My colleague has said that there is no stick. He is totally wrong. There is a very heavy stick. There is the stick of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. If the Member had attended the December 19 meeting of the legislative committee, he would have heard from Gordon
April 10, 1986

Fairweather, the Chairman of the Human Rights Commission, that we can enforce employment equity by enforcing the Canadian Human Rights Act. He said that we can initiate complaints, examine data and plans, and then appoint tribunals which have the authority to impose sanctions.
Mr. Fairweather also said, as have my colleagues, that some of the groups would like their own agencies to be there. There is enough fragmentation in the country now without dividing into a proliferation of boards, commissions, and agencies. We want to improve opportunity. Gordon Fairweather, who I know all Parties acknowledge for the pre-eminence of his work, supports this position. He said that we can do it.
One of my colleagues in the NDP said that a fine of $50,000 is peanuts. Maybe for the NDP $50,000 is peanuts, but for someone involved in business $50,000 is an awful lot of money. No company would want to be faced with the shame of being brought before an inquiry, with the cost involved in such an inquiry, or with the public shame of receiving a fine which would not look very good on their bottom line when they have to report to their shareholders and the public.
My colleagues on this side of the House have worked hard. This Bill does provide mandatory sanctions and a mandatory system of enforcement. However, I do not know why we spend so much time on this issue because, more importantly, the Bill provides the new thrust and thinking which will achieve employment equity for women, natives, racial minorities, and the handicapped in this country. I applaud this Bill and am happy to have been a part of it.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with interest to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins). She mentioned that she believes in the carrot. I know that Bugs Bunny believes in carrots, but I do not, nor does my Party. What we really need is a big stick in this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Bugs Bunny turned 50 the other day and what happened?

Bugs Bunny turned 50? He still likes carrots, but I do not.
There is no question, as we have said over and over again in committee and in this House, that this Bill must be strengthened if it is going to achieve the goals of equal opportunity in the workplace for women, native people, visible minorities and the disabled. There is no way we can expect movement in this direction unless the federal Government sets the example. We need a Bill which is far more comprehensive. It should affect a far greater number of employers and employees. It should have real teeth so we can have real enforcement of affirmative action or employment equity as the term is used in this Bill.
I am really rather amused by the amendment we are speaking to because it attempts to define the Bill as it really is. In its original state the Bill refers to the goal of achieving
Employment Equity
employment equity. As my colleague has pointed out through this amendment, it will not achieve employment equity. It is aiming at promoting, encouraging and persuading a few large companies which do business with the Government to give more attention to employment equity.
It will be very interesting to see how Conservative Members vote on this amendment. Are they going to vote in favour of our amendment which describes the Bill as it actually is? Or are they going to go back to the existing wording in the Bill? I hope that in the time remaining they take action with the Minister to try to change the Bill to strengthen it so it will have some real meaning. As it is now, it is just paying lip service. It will really be regressive to raise people's expectations only to find that in practical terms it cannot work.
My colleagues have also talked about the things we object to in the Bill. All the target groups who appeared in committee, I refer particularly to the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, as well as the coalition groups, the CLC and many trade unions-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I would hope Hon. Members will give the Hon. Member an opportunity to speak. I love to listen to her expound on this particular Bill and I would hope the other Members would, too.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate the wisdom with which you listen to these profound remarks I am making and I also thank my colleagues for listening.
I was saying that many groups will be affected by employment equity or the lack thereof. There were many women's groups, groups of the disabled, trade union and labour groups, as well as various representatives of native groups, including the Assembly of First Nations, and certainly other groups concerned with race relations and muiticulturalism. I know there was a consensus among them all that this Bill was not strong enough. It did not have the teeth to enforce the stated goal of achieving employment equity. There is no effective enforcement mechanism. The only penalty is one of $50,000 if a designated employer fails to report. Even just providing a picture of what their business is, is hardly achieving employment equity in a very real sense.
We have also expressed a number of objections about the kind of myths the Minister has put forward. Sometimes I wonder if she really understands what mandatory affirmative action is. I really feel that she does not comprehend it. I have respect for her, I think her motives are very strong and she wants to do something for the target groups we are talking about. However, she brought in an amendment which provides an action plan for employers. It was added after all the various groups objected that there was no enforcement. However, it is just words because there is no enforcement. There is no penalty for the employers who do not adhere to the plan. What is the point in putting it in? It is, once again, just platitudes.
I cannot believe that the Minister did not listen, but she did not seem to comprehend what organized labour is saying.

April 10, 1986
Employment Equity
These are the people who work in these large corporations. The CLC and various other labour groups have said over and over again that employment equity must be negotiated. It must be part of the collective bargaining process.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Must be negotiated?

What does the Minister do about that? She brought in some reference to token consultation with unions. I see the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) is here. You cannot really blame the labour movement for really being very angry about this. This is undercutting the whole collective bargaining process. There must be negotiations involving employment equity and all employees must be involved.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Negotiations? What happened to the big stick?

The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) comes from Manitoba. I wish he would stand up and tell us about the pay equity Bill which the Manitoba Government brought in. That is an attempt to put into legislation equal pay for work of equal value. Judge Abella strongly advocated that this must be part of the legislation. The NDP tried to present amendments here and they were rejected. There is no contract compliance which requires every company doing business with the Government to practise employment equity. There is no penalty if they do not. This Bill only applies to a few very large employers. There are probably only about three or four in British Columbia who will even be affected. Again, all they have to do is to report.
Another thing I want to stress, something to which Judge Abella made reference, and I have not heard other speakers referring to it, is that Judge Abella said that for there to be employment equity for employees in Government and private industry, there must be access to child care for parents who are workipg. If they do not have affordable access to child care suited to their shifts or their hours of work, they do not have equal opportunity in the workplace. They certainly do not have equal opportunity for promotion.
We have travelled from the Atlantic to the Pacific and back again. Everyone is asking us to do something about the crisis in child care. One of the things that should be done is to have more access to workplace child care and the federal Government has given no attention to that whatsoever. There has been no attention given to training opportunities. People who know about affirmative action say you must have opportunities to upgrade people, especially women and disadvantaged people, so they have a chance to move into other kinds of better paying, promotional jobs. It is an inadequate Bill and I feel very sorry that in this first attempt we have not made a better job of it.

Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable reluctance that I rise to speak to the question and the amendment before the House.
First of all, what we want is to obtain equality for all Canadian men and women: equality as such and equal access. However, this Bill is a sham.

Mr. Speaker, although I would like to support the Bill as it stands, assume and hope that it would achieve employment equity, there is no way the content of this Bill will enable people who are suffering at this point from a lack of equal access and equal opportunity to bring to the workforce their talents and skills.
We do have, unfortunately, a systemic discrimination that is indigenous to our workforce. The goal of employment equity is real and it is practical. It is a distant goal that is not going to be realized for those people who really need it.
I listened to the Parliamentary Secretary and the Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), both of whom 1 had assumed had a much larger heart and a bigger understanding of the issues. It is with a deep sense of regret that I listened to both of them. On the one hand the Parliamentary Secretary talks about the fact that he is a witness to what discrimination can do. I can speak as well from the same perspective. On the other hand the Member for Capilano spent six months with me travelling across this land and was witness, as I was, to the testimony of one group after the other who, unlike my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Weiner), and myself, have lived the experiences that we heard about. We have not had to live our life being deprived of earnings, which has a negative impact on our life and our ability to raise our family and give them the things we would love to give them. This would apply to native people in this country, the aboriginal peoples, the blacks in this country, or any of the other visible minority groups and some of the nonvisible minority groups as well as the handicapped who are looked at constantly based on their disability rather than their abilities.
I wish the Parliamentary Secretary had come along; maybe he would not have spoken the way he did. I regret that the Member for Capilano, who did come along, did speak the way she did. The reality is that there are few industries upon which this Bill will impact. We have had a sensitization of our population to this problem by Judge Abella. She is a very fine spokesman, extraordinarily articulate, and she made her voice heard. She said that voluntary action has not worked. Appeal to the hearts and minds does not impact on the people who are included in our concept of non-discrimination and equal opportunity in the workforce. From what I heard I can only tell you that we have missed the boat, and it is sad. The potential was there. I think the Minister wanted to realize her goals, but I think she was blocked at every turn by big business and by the corporate sector which, if you read the Nielsen task
April 10, 1986

force Report, indicate quite clearly that they did not want this Bill to be mandatory and they were not at all interested in seeing it applied in its fullest measure. 1 am sorry to say she has had to cave in.
One of the disappointments in this Government is the breaking of the promises that were so glibly falling from the tongue of our charming Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). In the Throne Speech the Prime Minister stated, and 1 quote him, "economic equality is the vehicle through which women-", and he is referring here, of course, to a lovely target market, 52 per cent of whom were supposed to buy his promise, and I continue my quote, "-will come to full partnership and participation with men in our society". These are very laudable principles, and words are very simple, but a law is another matter.
I would suggest to you that this law has no mechanisms to effect what we want in principle and in practice through equality. Judge Abella said that employment equity is a strategy designed to obliterate the present and residual effects of discrimination and to open equitably the competition for employment opportunities to those arbitrarily excluded. It requires a special blend of what is necessary, what is fair and what is workable. Obviously what was necessary, fair and workable did not work to date. In order for it to become workable you have to have a law that has teeth, otherwise it is a law in name only and it is a farce and a joke. To play games with our visible minorities, with our handicapped, with the ethnics, with the native people is a sham, and you should be ashamed of yourselves.
Hear, hear!
You are wrong.

You may think I am wrong, but it is you who are wrong.
I bring to your attention that when an evaluation was done in New York on the impact of the affirmative action program, which was mandatory in the United States, the analysis was, and I quote Victoria Smith, the senior consultant in New York, that, "Business is comfortable with numerical goals and targets. That is how business works. We just did surveys of our clients and most of them are Fortune 500 big corporations, they are now Fortune 1000, and of 142 responses 95 per cent said they would keep on using numerical goals to track the progress of women and minorities regardless of government requirements".
She went on to say that first you have to get them to understand that we are not imposing on them something that is anathema. The focus and the goal of employment equity is to bring the talents and potential of individuals to enrich our business community. It is not to punish them because we wish to give equal opportunity to those people who were discriminated because of the systemic barriers that need to be revised and reviewed.
Employment Equity
1 think it is about time that our federal Government, its agencies, Crown corporations, the federally operated and regulated sectors, and companies doing business with Government start to recognize the diversity of Canada's population and the potential of these disadvantaged people. This Bill demonstrates that this Government lacks the willpower and the leadership that is needed to implement employment equity programs effectively. I can only ask the Parliamentary Secretary to go back and read what the Canadian Ethnocultural Council has said or the coalition of provincial organizations for the handicapped. They are all disappointed with this Bill. I would specifically direct the Parliamentary Secretary to take a look at a research piece that was done in his own area. How will he respond to the Jamaican Association of Montreal? We have 18,000 Jamaicans and the statistics are quite astounding. There is a 69 per cent unemployment factor for 18 to 25 year olds; 41.5 per cent unemployment for those between the ages of 25 and 35; 31 per cent unemployment for those aged 35 to 45; 22 per cent unemployment for those between the ages of 45 and 60; and over 43 per cent unemployment for those aged 60 and over. That takes only the Jamaican community of Montreal into account, not including Haitians, Vietnamese or the handicapped. It is a shame. Tell me how this Bill will answer the needs of those people. It will not.
Employment equity deals with many things, including education, child care, re-education and training. Many activities are required and this Bill will not meet the needs of those members of his constituency, mine or that of anyone else in this country. It is with a deep regret that I indicate that we on this side of the House are not satisfied with this Bill.
There is no such thing as voluntary compliance according to affirmative action laws right now. A law without teeth is not a law. If voluntary compliance worked, then Moses would have come down from the mountain with the 10 guidelines.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to Motion No. 1 in the name of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton- Melville (Mr. Nystrom), to amend Bill C-62. This Bill is purportedly designed to achieve equality in the workplace. The amendment attempts to change that to read:
The purpose of this Act is to promote and encourage-
-equality in the workplace. This motion recognizes the particular lack of enforcement provisions that would be required to achieve employment equity and, therefore, justifies our proposing that the Bill is designed only to promote and encourage employment equity. It is a fair description of the Bill and it is particularly important to recognize that this is the extent to which the Government plans to take action. I believe that various groups in Canada hope that the Government will do more; which leads one to question how one views this particular Bill. We trust that the Bill will provide the necessary information to undertake additional action through various forms of compliance with the required enforcement to

April 10, 1986
Employment Equity
ensure that employment equity is actually achieved. The information provided in this Bill is certainly necessary in achieving that goal, and these groups will argue that the Bill should be passed so that the Government can introduce additional measures to meet the criticisms that my colleagues have already put forward and which I will consider as well.
The fact is that the Government does not intend to do anything more. There has been enough dicussion about the need for enforcement mechanisms to be included in the Bill.
A few minutes ago the Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) made a fine argument for depending on carrots. It is similar to what a Liberal Leader of the Opposition in the 1890s called "sunny ways", against the harsh measures that a Conservative Government was trying to bring to bear on the Province of Manitoba. One can celebrate sunny ways and one can enjoy carrots almost as much as Bugs Bunny has during his 50 year career, but the sad fact of the matter is that human beings frequently need a little more pressure than that.
The corporations to which this Bill will apply are those with more than 200 employees and having sales to the Government amounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Those corporations in particular will require some pressure, but the Government does not plan to bring any of that pressure to bear because once the Bill is passed-as the Government will presumably ensure-and the reporting begins, the Government will argue that several years must pass before we have any real basis to say that on the evidence of the reports they failed to act. The Government will argue that we must let that time pass before we envisage bringing in any substantial pressure to bear on these companies.
There will be a great deal of disappointment and anguish across the country in the next two or three years because there is no doubt that we will not see any enforcement provisions before the end of the Government's mandate in 1988 or 1989. Furthermore, there will be no action to meet the other criticisms that I will explain in a moment. Undoubtedly we will hear many fine intentions. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) makes that kind of speech very well. The Parliamentary Secretary is undoubtedly an honourable person and speaks to the need to achieve employment equity. I am sure that other Government Members can state those intentions very well too, but the Government does not intend to ensure that employment equity takes place.
It will depend on the Human Rights Commission, which is an independent body. I fear that when amendments to strengthen the Canadian Human Rights Act are introduced sometime in the next year or 18 months, they will not include some of the provisions that are needed so that the Canadian Human Rights Commission-the only enforcement means envisaged by the Government-will have the authority to ensure that employment equity will make progress. It is clear that this Bill does not provide the means to achieve employment equity but is undoubtedly designed to promote and encourage employment equity.
Let me point out some of the more specific weaknesses in the Bill. I have already commented on the lack of enforcement mechanisms. The most the Bill provides for is a $50,000 fine to those who fail to file reports. The Bill should have included provisions that take into account how a workforce reflects the local labour force, including the number of women in the workforce or who want to be in the workforce, the number of native people and visible minorities who live in the area and would like to find employment, as well as the number of disabled who are seeking employment. As the evidence mounts that these companies have not employed these people, we will only have the effect of public opinion on the Government.
In a week when we have been considering Bill C-91 relating to competition, I am reminded of other Governments that thought public opinion would do a great deal. The Combines Investigation Act is a splendid example of that. The best that could be said for William Lyon Mackenzie King in his day is that if companies were exposed as combining with others to constrain trade in order to drive prices up, to take from consumers more than those consumers should have to pay, and if he thought public opinion would make any difference, there is a lot of evidence that it did not in fact happen. Although fines are assessed against companies these days for a variety of offences, there is no lack of evidence to show that when companies are found guilty, they pay these fines and presumably go on their way, which leaves us to appreciate the fact that the lack of enforcement mechanism is a very serious flaw in the Act.
The first words in Clause 2 of the Bill, "to achieve equality in the workplace" makes this Bill unworthy because of the fact that it refers to the "workplace" in general terms. The Bill does not not provide for federal Government Departments themselves who are, after all, fairly substantial as employers. One of the things we sought in committee was an expansion of the Bill to relate specifically to Departments of the Government. I fear that in this area the report of the special committee on the participation of visible minorities may deserve some part of the blame for what has happened. In the distinctions which were drawn in that report we have discussion of the need for "affirmative action", as the language was at that point. There was a section which related to the country generally and to the private sector, if you will, and then we have another part which related to Government and the needs of Government. I believe that if the Government of our day were really serious about achieving employment equity in the workplace, it would have ensured that the Bill applied to those Departments. It would have overcome the shortcomings of that aspect of the Equality Now Report and ensured that there was such an application.
For these reasons, among others, I support the amendment of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville that Clause 2 be amended to read "to promote and encourage", because that is the most that this Bill will do.
April 10, 1986

Mr. Speaker, 1 am also pleased to participate in the debate on report stage of Bill C-62. I would like to preface my remarks by recalling to the House a quote by Judge Abella, the architect and author of the Abella Commission Report. She said: "Unenforceable rights are no more satisfactory than unavailable rights". 1 think that speaks volumes about the malaise of Bill C-62. I believe it is the malaise of Bill C-62 to which Motion No. 1 refers itself. Following the presentation of the Abella Commission Report, which was a very courageous, forthcoming and progressive report, great expectations were created among Canadians and, more specifically, among the four target groups which the Abella Commission identified. There were great expectations that the Government of the day would take the window of opportunity and the momentum which was offered by the Abella Commission, by the Equality Now and Equality for All Reports and that somehow those recommendations and bold findings would be put into legislation. But neither the recommendations nor the findings are in Bill C-62.
Bill C-62 does not achieve employment equity. It only talks of and about employment equity. There is a world of difference between the two.
During second reading, Hon. Members on this side of the House asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to strengthen Bill C-62. It was hoped that at the committee stage, where we would be meeting with those four target groups and other Canadians interested in Bill C-62, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Government would see the merit and the reasons for strengthening such a Bill. Group after group, the Ethnocultural Council, the Urban Alliance for Race Relations from Toronto, women's groups, native groups and groups of the disabled, all came forward with hope in their hearts that the committee would grant equal opportunity not just to you and me, Mr. Speaker, but to those individuals. These groups appeared before committee and told Hon. Members from all Parties what they were seeking and had been seeking for years. It is not an easy process, nor is it an overnight process. It is a longterm difficult task. There should be no shortcuts nor the easy public relations gimmicks about which Bill C-62 speaks.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said so often on the hustings in 1984: "We will provide a Government for the people". If there is an absence of that promise, it is in Bill C-62. It is a piece of legislation which says that we are going to have basically four targets, women, natives, the handicapped and visible minorities. But those people came before the committee and before Members of Parliament in other forums, such as public meetings in Toronto, and said that they are not in agreement with Bill C-62. They told us that it falls short and will not do the things it says it will do. But those submissions fell on deaf ears. If this is a Government for the people, then the Government should at least have the decency to respond specifically and honourably to these requests and aspirations.
Employment Equity
Those groups have gone away with the hope that at report stage, at which we are now, the eleventh hour, the Government will address in a bold and courageous manner that which it said it would. There is a shortage of action between Bill C-62 and the Abella Commission Report. There were great expectations which once again have not been met.
As Members of Parliament, perhaps one of the most difficult things for us to tackle in terms of individual representations in our constituencies, are the requests of individuals seeking employment. Individuals come to their Members of Parliament and say: "Look, 1 have not had a job in the last year. I have put in X number of applications and the answer is always the same. Would you please try to help me?" We, as Members of Parliament, try to do our utmost to assist those constituents. What is more hurtful is to have individuals within the four target groups come to us and suggest they are being denied opportunities of employment because of who they are or because of their handicaps. That hurts deeply. It is the dignity of work which I believe gives definition to one's self worth. It is having employment which gives one the hope of carrying on and providing for one's family. But when a black Canadian, a handicapped Canadian, a native Canadian or a woman come to us and tell us they are being discriminated against based on their particular traits, we must feel that this is something that should not happen in this country. It should not happen with our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Yes, Canada is a great country. We all realize that we have no peer in terms of our greatness. However, we should not end the debate there. There are a large number of Canadians who unfortunately cannot concur with those sentiments. Some Canadians are saying that the opportunities that exist for their neighbours or for people in other provinces do not exist for them. As long as that is the case, Canada does not mean to those people what it means to you and me, Mr. Speaker. That is why it is important for Bill C-62 to deal with opportunities in a forthright and courageous way and, perhaps, in the most challenging and difficult way.
It should be admitted that this problem is not an easy one to eradicate. However, that is not an excuse to give the issue only some PR and patchwork. There is no excuse for doing that. We should have built on the momentum of the findings of the various reports to which I have referred. We should have built on the representations that these four communities made not only during the constitutional process and the making of the Equality for Now Report but during the Abella Commission hearings. The Government is not delivering the goods.
It is no wonder that we are hearing representatives of these individual groups saying that they are losing faith and trust in the system. They have been telling the system to change for the last number of years. Here in Parliament we have the window of opportunity open that would allow us to make the lot of these four groups better, but I am ashamed to be a part of a Parliament that is presenting Bill C-62. That is why I was

April 10, 1986
Employment Equity
astounded when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister rose to say that April 10 is a great day and he is proud. What is he proud of? Why do we not ask members of the four target groups if they are proud of the Government? Does the Parliamentary Secretary understand the struggles of those Canadians day after day or, in some cases, generation after generation?
We should not be proud of Bill C-62. We should put it back on the drawing board. Motion No. 1 speaks to the malaise that has gripped Bill C-62. I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker, but it is my hope that following report stage, the Government will find some sensitivity and will be progressive rather than simply do a PR job on what is a very fundamental issue for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this Bill. But before 1 do so, Mr. Speaker, noticing you in the chair, I would say that I was severely critical of 21 Alberta MPs for not speaking out on another matter the other day. I would like to make that 20 MPs and certainly exclude you, Mr. Speaker.
Order.
Well, then, 19. Are there any more? Let me speak on this Bill. It is important-
Shame on you.

I invite the Hon. Member to rise to speak on this Bill if he wants to reply. Unfortunately, unlike the Hon. Member, I cannot speak while seated. We know where the brains of the Tories are. They are better when they are sitting on them.
This Bill is supposed to be about employment equity. I think the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) summed it up very neatly when he said that the Bill talks about employment equity and looks as if it were about employment equity but does not really do very much about employment equity. He outlined the four major groups that have made submissions to the Government over three inquiries, one commission and one constitutional hearing, namely, women, visible minorities, natives and the disabled. Apparently the Government was not listening to them. Certainly if it had been listening, there would have been a much stronger Bill with some teeth and enforcement provisions presented to the House.
Let us confess, we all like the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) a great deal. However, I have picked up from the debate that Hon. Members feel that she kind of struck out in Cabinet. That is an appropriate metaphor as baseball season is just beginning. Flora got up to bat and struck out in Cabinet. This Bill certainly will not do effectively that which we believe the Minister of Employment and Immigration would like to do, giving her the benefit of the doubt, and that is, to bring in a Bill that will give a sense of equity and fairness to Canadians who are not in an equal position.
In French!

My hon. friend asks me to speak French. Well, the problem is the same for Quebec as it is for other regions in Canada. The problem is exactly the same, and that is why I intend to continue in English.

We have to ask ourselves why the Government has watered down this Bill and the policy of real equality.
Because they are Conservatives.

Exactly, because it is a Conservative Government. As we can see by the competition Bill, and with only a few exceptions, this is a Government that is in tune with the wealthy and big business interests. Its relentless pursuit of tax increases, elimination of jobs, protection of the wealthy minority, taxes on old age pensioners, taxes on pensionable UIC recipients and cut-backs on social services for the needy show the basic thrust of the Government. We can see evidence of that in the competition Bill, a sweetheart Bill for business, and this Bill, a backtracking Bill that does not really deal with employment equity.
In Proverbs, chapter 22:16, the Bible says:
He that oppresseth the poor to increase his riches, and he that givcth to the rich, shall surely come to want.
In spite of today's opinion polls, I predict that if the Government continues on this path, it too will surely come to want, if not in heaven then at the next election.
There are ways to deal with the flaws in this Bill. It could be made stronger. Women are members of one group that is affected. Employment equity pertains basically to women. They are the ones who are unequal in the workplace. All sorts of commissions have said that, and some eloquent speeches have been made by some of the women opposition Members today. I need not repeat them.
This Bill will not have the tough enforcement procedures we need to make equality a reality. It will not come overnight. We have to have some enforcement procedures and some specific goals and targets. Again, there have to be ways of enforcing those goals and targets. The Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) spoke about possible effective enforcement procedures in some detail.
Visible minorities form another group that will be affected. In my riding, there are many Chinese Canadians, probably more than in any other riding. In many ways, Chinese Canadians are now receiving a measure of equality and acceptance that they never have in the past, mainly through their own efforts but also through a change in attitudes on the part of the people of British Columbia. In the past, there were race riots in British Columbia. The stores of Chinese Canadians were burned. A recent survey taken in British Columbia revealed that British Columbians had become one of the most tolerant people in Canada. That is real progress. The Chinese

struggled to get that equality. 1 am not pleased to say that the place which Chinese Canadians used to occupy is now occupied by East Indians who are a very visible minority in the southeast part of Vancouver, especially Sikhs who wear turbans and so on. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to rise to speak in support of Bill C-62. Much has been said about it this afternoon. For a moment or two I should like to refer to the contents of the Bill itself. Its purpose is defined as follows:
-to achieve equality in the workplace so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and. in the fulfilment of that goal, to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the same way but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences.
I hope it is clear to everyone that the target groups are women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada.
In that Your Honour is from Edmonton, I think you would be the first to agree that southeast Edmonton contains large numbers of people in the target groups. It may surprise Hon. Members opposite to know that in Edmonton-Strathcona 62 per cent of the people living there are of origin other than British or French. As was stated so eloquently by the Hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Weiner), this is a step forward in Canada. It is the first time in our entire history that a Government has done something about employment equity. It is a day of which all of us in the House should be proud. I, for one, am very proud to be associated with a Government which is doing this.
It is self-evident that the target groups are not given the same opportunities as other Canadians. I recall being in Montreal a couple of years ago when it was pointed out to me that the unemployment rate among visible minorities in that city was in excess of 20 per cent. It is an unfortunate fact of life in Canada that people in the target groups do not have the same opportunities as have other Canadians. If my Party believes in anything, it is that we believe in equality of

April 10, 1986
Employment Equity
opportunity for all Canadians including the four targeted groups,
Certainly you do, David.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
It is not perfect, but I ask my close friend, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), what has any other Government in our history done in this regard? I think the answer, in fairness, would be, absolutely nothing.
I should like to deal with some of the points raised by Hon. Members opposite. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal referred to employment statistics on visible minorities and to Canadians of Jamaican origin. For the first time employers in Montreal and elsewhere will be required to implement equity and demonstrate the results of their efforts. For the first time those employers will have to account to the people of Canada and to the Canadian Human Rights Commission which will take action if companies fail to show positive results. As 1 understand it, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) stated that she did not like the enforcement question. The Canadian Human Rights Commission will monitor progress under the Bill. I understand the commission appeared before the committee and indicated that it fully supported the proposed enforcement process and that it would continue to monitor the progress made. The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) indicated that public opinion, as 1 understand it, was not important in the achievement of employment equity. To what do any of us answer? It is public opinion, and 1 am not referring to those days when we do well in a public opinion poll. Public opinion is the governing factor in a democracy, and I hope it always will be.
I listened to the remarks of the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi). I would ask him: Which recommendations in the excellent Abella Report we are not attempting to deal with? My parents and his ancestors came to Canada with hope. In my view we must all start at the same point on the starting line and compete together. However, the reality is that the target groups in the Bill all too often do not have the same opportunity. We are determined on this side of the House- and I hope that is the case for those on his side-to ensure that Canada takes this very significant step forward today.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate. There have been a number of facetious and fallacious statements made by Government Members. It is unfortunate that they do not know the facts. They do not know that this particular so-called step forward has been criticized by every group and every organization involved in the search for equality and for minorities.
It is also pretty clear, as stated by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), that the heavyweights in the Conservative Cabinet put their foot down and blocked any move toward real equality for women. It is very clear that some of those heavyweights do not believe in equality for women.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) is the Minister responsible for the implementation of the equality report. Let us look at what the Minister of Justice thinks about women and what he thinks about equality even in this very august Chamber. At a fund raising dinner a couple of weeks ago, the Minister of Justice made his comment very clear, Mr. Speaker. An article in a newspaper, in part, reads:
Saying federal opposition MPs presented "strong arguments for retroactive birth control" and likening Liberal MP Sheila Copps to a codfish, federal Justice Minister John Crosbie was on the attack-
One of his more venemous attacks made against Ms. Copps. After describing a codfish as having a "stupid looking face" with a mouth that is "usually wide open," he went on to say: "The perfect example of a codfish would be Sheila Copps."
The Minister of Justice who said that the opposition Parties are the greatest justification for retroactive birth control is, in fact, the same Minister who is responsible for the implementation of equality. If Members on the Government side of the House had taken the time to read the equality report, they would know that in the report itself there is an absolute and direct challenge levelled at the Government with respect to the employment equity Bill.
The equality committee, made up of a majority of Conservatives, studied the laws of the land, including the proposed Bill we are discussing today, and found that this particular legislation did not meet the needs of women, did not meet the needs of minorities and was a violation of the principles of equality. Why is it still a violation of the principles of equality?
First, built into the legislation is a clause that states that all federal agencies covered under the Financial Administration Act will not be covered by this Bill. In one fell swoop, with one stroke of the pen, the federal Government has introduced a Bill which does not apply to the RCMP, to the Canadian Armed Forces or to any federal Government agencies which are directly under the rubrick of Treasury Board. It only applies to federally regulated companies. To boot, Mr. Speaker, all federally regulated companies are not covered under this legislation. Only approximately 100 of over 30,000 federal companies will be covered by this legislation. Approximately 100 companies, and the balance, over 30,000 companies, can thumb their noses at the Government and can tell the Government that they will continue to pursue the voluntary approach which has proven in the past not to work.
Even though this measure covers only 100 companies, it will target a number of employees within federally regulated bodies, such as the banks and various transportation industries, and for that we would give them a great round of applause if the Bill said anything. The Bill should say, "You have targets which you must reach, otherwise the federal Government, through the auspices of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, will step in and do something". There is no requirement upon any company to do anything. All that is asked of a company is to send in an annual report on its progress.
April 10, 1986

How will those reports be monitored? An audit, a random audit which would lead to absolutely no response or no conditions on the companies at all. We have heard over and over again in the House of Commons today from a number of Members who should know better. I think of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), who was presumably informed on the issue since she spent the better part of last year criss-crossing the country, studying questions and saying that nothing had been done under previous Liberal Governments. I would like to set the record straight, Mr. Speaker.
Those of us in Parliament realize that under any Government the progress we have made is not enough, but it is pretty important that the public recognize that in 1971 Canada became the first country in the western world to recognize women at the highest levels of decision making by establishing a cabinet position for women. In 1973, a non-governmental advisory council on the status of women was established. In 1972, the federal Government ratified the International Labour Organization's convention concerning equal pay for work of equal value, even though the current Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) with respect to the labour dispute in Newfoundland has made it quite clear that the Government does not intend to respect the ILO convention signed by previous Liberal Governments. In 1975 there was the introduction of an omnibus Bill to provide equality of status for women. In 1976, we had the adoption of the Canadian Human Rights Act forbidding discrimination on the basis of sex. In 1978, we had an amendment to the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the equal splitting of pension credits and amendments to the Canada Labour Code to eliminate pregnancy as a basis for lay-off or dismissal. In 1982, we had the Charter of Rights and Freedoms over the dead body of a particular Progressive Conservative Premier of a certain province in Canada. Over his dead body the federal Liberal Party introduced the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which guaranteed equal rights to men and women, including an override clause, which was blocked at every step by Conservatives across the nation.
When we talk about equality, let us look at the question of unemployment benefits, which has a direct bearing on how we can seek equality in the workforce. We know right now that the federal Conservative Party, the Government sitting across the way, is looking at taking pregnancy leave out of unemployment insurance benefits. It is one of the things being studied by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
When the Liberal Government introduced pregnancy leave as a right through unemployment insurance, as with other types of leave which were not covered under the Searching for Work section, it was introduced because Liberals believed and continue to believe that in order to give women the opportunity to compete equally in the workforce they have to have an opportunity of access to child care, access to bearing a child without being penalized and without fear of losing their jobs, without financial hardship and disability. It seems to me that
Employment Equity
what we have here is a Government that is sending the women of Canada a double-whammy.

It is a well-known fact, Mr. Speaker, that many ministers in this Government, in this Cabinet, have not the slightest interest in achieving equality for women. We also know that as far as this Bill is concerned, all groups, including women, minority groups, racial minorities, all those groups have already told the Government that the Bill does not meet the needs of Canadian men and women. Not just the ethnic groups and visible minorities and women's groups have voiced their disapproval. The Conservative Committee said in the report on equality that Bill C-62 went against the principles of equity as previously defined in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
If Progressive Conservative Members would take the time to read the Charter, they would see why the Committee was unanimous in demanding that the Government change the Bill, and the reason is that the Bill as tabled fails to provide for Government responsibility.
For instance, most companies are not covered by the Bill, including the Government, including the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which has been said to discriminate against Francophones. Today, the Canadian Forces fail to respect the equality of women as far as career opportunities in the Armed Forces are concerned. All these groups are not covered by the Bill because the Government, or rather the Minister-1 suppose as a result of the enormous influence of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen)-has decided to eliminate all the groups included in the Financial Administration Act. In other words, Government employees will not have the same rights as employees in the private sector, before the federal Government.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear there are incredible deficiencies, and if Progressive Conservative Members are truly interested in equality for women, they should reject the Bill in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, as 1 listened to the remarks of the Minister when she introduced this Bill and to those of the Parliamentary Secretary, I could only conclude that either they are completely ignorant of how the real world of employment operates, or they are involved in a charade trying to fool the Canadian people into believing they are doing something when, in fact, they are not.
In terms of employment, the fate of four important groups will be vitally affected by the effectiveness of this Bill. Those groups have expressed their opposition because they know from experience that without targets and numerical goals being set in the Act, nothing will happen. I refer to women, natives, the handicapped, and people from the visible minorities.

April 10, 1986
Employment Equity
I heard the Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) say that 62 per cent of his constituents come from neither Anglo Saxon nor French origin. That Member grew up in Winnipeg and he will know that the percentage is even higher in my constituency. 1 had the opportunity to work for a dozen years with the labour movement, ethnic groups, and community organizations in precisely this area of how to deal in Canada with the problems of prejudice and discrimination.
In the 1950s we suggested to Governments, federal and provincial, that legislation was needed to stop employers from refusing to hire people because of their race, religion, or colour. We heard all kinds of lectures about the fact that legislation would not work. We were told that legislation would only exacerbate the prejudices and that we needed education. After a few years of really studying the problem, the Government realized that legislation was needed.
I give credit to the first Government to enact such legislation in the form of the Fair Employment Practices Act, the then Conservative Government of Ontario lead by Mr. Frost. Some years later, when we went to work on the question of accommodations, we were able to prove that there were hotels, summer resorts, and even districts in certain cities, which made it impossible, or very uncomfortable, for people to get accommodation because of their race, colour, or creed. We then had passage of the Fair Accommodation Practices Act.
We are told that all we need do is to encourage people. The federal Liberal Government targeted certain Departments. It said that it believed in making employment for minority groups easier. It targeted certain Departments to hire people from minority groups. The record was very poor. I am not saying that that Government did not want a better record and did not try. However, it is easy to pass legislation or announce policies, but if the personnel managers do not believe in it, it simply will not work, and it has not worked.
If one studies the Departments which were targeted by the former Government to make progress, one sees that there was very little progress. How many natives and other non-white people work for the federal Government? How many women are there in senior executive positions? There are very few, although our universities have graduated large numbers of women lawyers and doctors and some women engineers and architects. They are not working for Governments because the personnel managers have not been convinced that they ought to do this, and we have not set goals.
The United States has had a great deal of experience in this area. Under the Johnson and Carter administrations, legislation very similar to ours was passed. However, they set goals and targets, and those targets were monitored. The American Government is now headed by the most pro-business President that the United States has had in 50 years. The present Government is against legislation and regulations which interfere with the rights of businesses to make decisions which they think are right for themselves. They have been considering getting rid of these targets. This is a very interesting situation. Even though they are ideologically committed to
getting rid of these targets and goals, the Secretary of Labour, Mr. Brock, is telling President Reagan that they should keep the goals and targets.
In addition to Secretary of Labour Brock, representatives of the National Association of Manufacturers in the United States, the major organization representing the major business corporations in the United States, have said openly, clearly, and on the record to the President of the United States that they do not want those numbers to be eliminated. They have explained it very simply by saying that as long as the Government sets targets and tells them clearly and precisely what they are required to do by way of bringing more equity into the workforce, hiring more people who are non-white, native, handicapped, and women, they are prepared to do it. They feel that there will be no doubts or difficulties and that they will not be criticized in the future for not having done the right thing. If that is what the American business community has learned through experience, surely Canadian business and industry would come to the same conclusion if given the opportunity and requirement.
I go into the banks, supermarkets, and major retail stores in my city of Winnipeg. We have thousands of non-white citizens in Winnipeg. I challenge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), who comes from my province, to come to Winnipeg, as I am sure he does, and to go, as I do, into any of those establishments. Mr. Speaker, you would have to look for a long time and wear very large magnifying glasses before you would see a few, if any, people who are non-white, handicapped, or native, working in any of those places. The record of my city Government is no better. There has been a long campaign to try to get the Winnipeg Police Department to hire a few native people, a few Filipinos, a few Sikhs. We have as well a very small percentage of women on the Winnipeg Police Force. When I use my city as an illustration, the record in other cities such as Montreal, Halifax, Toronto, Calgary, Edmonton or Vancouver is, I am certain, no better. Passage of this Bill without a requirement for targeting as well as provision for enforcement will make it a mockery and it will not work.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) wishes to participate in the debate?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The debate is on the motion to change the preamble of this Bill to "promote and encourage" rather than to "achieve". At first sight this amendment is almost trivial. However, 1 think it communicates something of importance, that being a recognition of the limitations of this legislation, which are considerable. It reminds us, too, of the limits of past legislation dealing with human rights. There have been a number of laws passed in this country the purpose of which in general has been to give the force of law to the notion that there ought to be accorded equal opportunity in the first instance to minority groups and, as our philosophy on equality evolved, to women, the disabled, natives and others. Never has any of this legislation achieved the purpose for which it was intended. It has always been a case of an effort to make progress along a path which has always proved to be far more difficult than people want.
Of course, this legislation is dramatic testimony to the failures of the past in attempting to achieve anti-discrimination legislation. At one time it was possible to hope that by saying it was against the law to discriminate in employment practices and providing a mechanism by which someone could enter a complaint, in the end employers would not discriminate. Of course it failed and ultimately led to a whole new point of view regarding anti-discrimination legislation, usually described as affirmative action. Therefore, even if you accept that this Bill was able to promote employment equity or affirmative action, the fact is that it has none of the requirements which are essential to achieving that end.
It is to mislead the public and the target groups to suggest that this Bill promotes that goal, because it lacks so much. Even were it to contain every necessary element, the essential purpose of the Bill could not be described as any more than promoting and encouraging employment equity. Therefore, to suggest this amendment is to do nothing more than to suggest that the English language be used properly.
Of course, there are more substantial difficulties with this Bill. These have been enumerated on many occasions. The claim that it does achieve or even promote employment equity or affirmative action dissolves into nothingness when you realize that all it really does is to demand that employers determine the numbers of minority groups or target groups in an employer's shop. That is fine, that is progress, but let us not make it any more than it is. It does not set any kind of penalty for failure to achieve some measure of equity. It has no targets, no timetables, and none of the things that just about everyone concerned, certainly the target groups, have demanded.
Employment Equity
I have many opportunities to talk in particular to members of visible minority organizations and many who are not part of any organization at all. Many of them have lived in this country for many, many years, watching a moving target. That moving target is to achieve equality and equal opportunity not only in employment but in a number of other areas. This Bill specifically deals with employment. In Toronto, for example, the Urban Alliance discovered two things in two studies, first, that members of visible minority groups have one-third the chance of the majority population of even getting as far as an interview. The same survey found that many employers, without provocation and quite spontaneously, uttered the most awful stereotypical and negative comments and views about members of visible minorities.
We were told in an earlier intervention that this Bill imposes a really serious requirement in its demand for enumeration, that to impose anything more would be to increase the degree of factionalism in this country and increase division. I have never heard a more absurd argument. What could be more divisive or faction-generating than that significant portions of our population, something of the order of half a million citizens of this country, should have the perception that they have one-third the chance of the general population of getting access to ordinary jobs in a city which historically has been regarded as one of the best urban areas with regard to access to opportunity? Many of these people have watched effort after effort to implement anti-discrimination legislation only to see such legislation fail. Often the legislation has been excellent for its time. The anti-discrimination legislation of Ontario led the continent. The anti-discrimination legislation and its implementation in Nova Scotia became the symbol for the world of the success of that kind of an effort. No matter how successful this good legislation was, it failed. It failed because attitudes hardened and practices developed that made discrimination more subtle, and now is the time for change. Everyone who has looked at the issue knows that the only approach is through affirmative action programs which are mandatory and enforced. This Bill, therefore, lacks its essential quality to provide affirmative action and employment equity which are mandatory and have teeth.
This is a toothless wonder that disappoints the minority groups of this country and it is far too long that they have been disappointed in their goal of achieving a nation in which equity, fairness and opportunity are accorded to them in the way that history has given them cause to earn.

1 would like to support the amendment that has been put forward because I think it is more in keeping with what is going to be achieved if Bill C-62 is passed. There is nothing in this Bill to indicate that the purpose of the act of achieving, as it is presently stated, equality in the workplace can possibly be realized. It is a Bill of statements and a Bill of wishes, but nothing that would indicate anything in the area of what is

April 10, 1986
Employment Equity
going to be achieved. Neither is there any indication or likelihood that it will be achieved unless this Government brings forward some proper sanctions.
1 think the idea of the Bill and the statement of what we would like to see brought forward and achieved in it is a laudable one, and I commend the Government for that. I am very much concerned that we have this Bill before the House at the present time, and we have stated what we would like to see achieved, but I am very concerned that it is not going to be achieved.
It has been said in debate in this House, "Well, here we have Bill C-62, and this is a start, this is something that we can build on, this is more than we have had before". I do not see it that way. I am concerned that the opposite will be the case, that by passing this Bill into law, Members of the House and the Government are going to say, "Well, that is that subject out of the way. We can put this question of employment equality aside for a while and get on to other things", when actually this matter has not been dealt with adequately.
To delude ourselves that this Bill is going to allow us to push this question aside and to get on with other things I think would be a travesty. In fact, there is so much that needs to be done for the visible minorities, women, native peoples and the handicapped that this Bill does not scratch the surface.
We are not even putting our own house in order as a federal Government and as a federal jurisdiction. The federal Departments and agencies are not all being brought under the auspices of this Bill. We have got to create an example in the federal jurisdiction. We have not done that and this Bill is not going to do it. If the Government is not going to set the example, how can the Government possibly expect others to adhere to what this Bill would like to see achieved?
None of the requests or objectives of the four minority groups that this Bill hopes to cover have been met. All four groups have appeared before the committee relating to this Bill and have asked for a stronger Bill, for more stringent provisions, and certainly sanctions that would allow this Bill to be followed the way we all would like to see it followed.
We owe a great deal in this country to the groups that are mentioned here, and I think that by giving this question such a cursory glance and such cursory attention we are really doing a disservice, not only to the groups but to our country. We have heard so often about the problems that exist with respect to the disabled. We have had an excellent task force on the disabled which presented a report during the last Parliament called Obstacles. I think it brought to our attention and to the attention of Canadians in a much more detailed fashion the problems facing the disabled today. The disabled have a right to achieve equal opportunity in the workplace and in the market-place.
We must certainly do a great deal more. I know we have given special attention to entrance and exit requirements, to special parking requirements, and to service requirements for the disabled, and these are very important. These have been
very sizeable steps in recent years. This Act does not complement these advances. This Act does not add anything further to what has been done, because what we need now is to be able to give the disabled the assurance that they are going to be treated fairly when it comes to gainful employment.
Another group that is mentioned here are native people. A great deal still needs to be done. Many of the problems have been historical problems that we have created. I think that trying to deal with the problems that have been created from past attempts, albeit very noble and well meaning attempts to deal with the needs of our native people, trying to address and correct these problems here with this Bill, is only going to make the situation worse. It is going to indicate to our native people that by bringing this Bill forward in the form that we have it we are not sincere, we just want to make a cosmetic attempt. This is wrong because it deserves much more attention.
What I have to say about the first two groups applies as well to the visible minorities and to women whose problems and needs have been emphasized and discussed already in the House. There is a great deal more that needs to be done. There needs to be some way of getting to the problems and ensuring that the problems are going to be corrected. We cannot let employment equity take place on an honour system. It is far too important. We must create an example by imposing sanctions to show that we, as parliamentarians, mean what we say and are determined to improve the situation of these groups.

Mr. Speaker, I know there are some Members who may be disappointed that the House is not ready for the question, but they will have to listen to one more speech and, hopefully, many more.
The Bill disappoints you.

I hear the cries of disappointment across the way and they bring joy to my heart because they indicate that we must continue the debate. Perhaps if we repeat the points that must be made government Members will begin to see the error of their ways and realize how this Bill is deficient. Perhaps they will decide to withdraw this Bill and introduce adequate legislation.
With new ideas.
More than anything else, the Government needs new ideas and new initiatives. It must begin to take real action on the problems facing Canadians.
They're Conservatives.

Of course, it comes as no surprise with a Conservative Government that it fails to take effective action
April 10, 1986

when it involves social justice and equality in Canadian society.
Although this employment equity Bill purports to have a mandatory affirmative action program, its compliance is essentially voluntary. Experience has shown that in order to have an effective affirmative action program it must be truly mandatory, which means there must be an enforcement mechanism to make sure that companies falling within the domain of this legislation will pay a price if they do not take the necessary action to ensure equality in the workplace. That penalty must be sufficient to encourage them to take the necessary action.
This legislation fails fundamentally because it does not have any teeth to enforce the policies of equality in the workplace between men, women, visible minorities, native people and the handicapped.
Enforcement mechanisms are necessary because the decisions made by companies are motivated by the ability to make profit from products that are marketable and competitive. Those companies face these pressures when making decisions on the allocation of their resources. If the Government expects these companies to bring about equality in the workplace, it must apply sufficient pressure to encourage them to introduce those programs.
One of the basic elements of an affirmative action program is enforcement. That mechanism is lacking in this Bill. Therefore, this legislation needs to be debated at length.
For at least another five minutes.

Given the quality of the legislation, five minutes would be a long time.
